directions: Section II, Question 1: Document-Based Question. Suggested time: 60 minutes (about 15 minutes reading and planning, 45 minutes writing). This question counts for 25 percent of your total score. It is mandatory. In your response you should: respond with a historically defensible thesis that establishes a line of reasoning; describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt; use at least six of the seven documents to support your argument, explaining how the documents' content supports it; explain the relevance of the point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience for at least two documents; and demonstrate a complex understanding by qualifying, corroborating, or modifying your argument.
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the Constitution led to political change in the United States from 1760 to 1800.

documents.text: In the House of Representatives there is not the substance but the shadow only of representation; which can never produce proper information in the legislature, or inspire confidence in the people; the laws will therefore be generally made by men little concerned in, and unacquainted with their effects and consequences.

rubric_map.thesis: 1 point: a historically defensible claim establishing a line of reasoning about the extent of political change caused by the Constitution (e.g., the Constitution fundamentally restructured American government by creating an energetic federal state, though continuities such as slavery and elite rule limited the change).
rubric_map.contextualization: 1 point: describe a broader historical context such as the imperial crisis and Revolution (British taxation, the failure of the Articles, Shays' Rebellion) that explains why a new frame of government was demanded.
rubric_map.evidence: 3 points: use the content of at least six documents to support the argument, with at least two documents explained in depth (e.g., Doc 1 shows the weak confederation the Constitution replaced; Doc 3 shows the new theory of checked federal power; Doc 4 shows Anti-Federalist fear that representation would be hollow; Doc 5 shows the Bill of Rights answering that fear; Doc 2 shows slavery's persistence as a limit on change; Doc 6 shows states'-rights resistance continuing under the new system; Doc 7 shows the new system's peaceful transfer of power).
rubric_map.sourcing: 1 point: explain the relevance of point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience for at least two documents (e.g., Doc 3: Madison writing as Publius to persuade New York ratifiers, so he stresses safeguards; Doc 4: Mason as a dissenting Convention delegate warning the public; Doc 6: Jefferson drafting a partisan state protest against Federalist overreach in the Quasi-War crisis).
rubric_map.complexity: 1 point: demonstrate complex understanding by qualifying or modifying the argument, for example by showing that the Constitution changed the structure of government while leaving slavery (Doc 2) and conflicts over federal power (Doc 6) unresolved, so the change was real but bounded.
